title: Use `Stream.peek` to log each employee as it passes a filtering and mapping pipeline, for auditing, without altering the elements. Explain what `peek` does, why it is an intermediate operation, and the caution about relying on it.
shortTitle: Audit each element flowing through a pipeline using peek without changing the data
keyPoints: peek(Consumer) performs a side effect on each element and passes it downstream unchanged
peek is an intermediate, lazy operation: nothing runs until a terminal operation pulls elements
Placed after a filter, peek observes only the elements that survived the filter
peek is intended for debugging and lightweight auditing, not for transforming data
An optimizing pipeline may skip peek when the result can be computed without visiting elements
Use map for real transformations and forEach for guaranteed terminal side effects
In parallel streams the peek Consumer must be thread-safe because it runs on many threads

s1_definition.oneliner: `peek` lets you watch each element go by for logging or auditing without modifying it; it is a side-effect window, not a transformer.
s1_definition.profdef:
peek is a narrow tool with one honest job: observe.

- **peek(Consumer)** – applies the consumer to each element as it flows past, then emits the same element unchanged to the next stage.
- **Intermediate and lazy** – the consumer runs only while a terminal operation pulls elements through the pipeline, so `stream().peek(...)` with no terminal does nothing.
- **Position matters** – a peek placed after a `filter` sees only the elements that passed the filter, so it is ideal for auditing survivors.
- **Debugging first** – the Stream contract says peek exists mainly to support debugging, not to carry essential logic.
- **May be skipped** – an optimizing pipeline can legally bypass peek when it can produce the result without visiting every element.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a conveyor belt of account forms at the National Bank of India. peek is a CCTV camera mounted over the belt: it photographs each form for the audit log as the form passes, but it never changes or removes a form. The forms continue down the belt exactly as they were. Priya the compliance officer trusts the camera to watch, but she would never ask it to approve a loan, because watching is all it is built to do.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
PEEK IN A PIPELINE: OBSERVE, DO NOT CHANGE

  source           filter            peek              map            collect
┌─────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────┐
│ staff   │──▶│ salary >     │──▶│ log the │──▶│ Employee     │──▶│ List of  │
│ stream  │   │ 1,000,000    │   │ survivor│   │ ::name       │   │ names    │
└─────────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────┘
                     │                │
                     ▼                ▼
               drops Priya      element unchanged,
               (800,000)        only logged


LAZY EXECUTION: NOTHING RUNS UNTIL THE TERMINAL PULLS

   stream().peek(...)              stream().peek(...).collect(...)
   ┌───────────────┐               ┌───────────────┐
   │ no terminal   │               │ terminal pulls│
   │ peek runs 0x  │               │ peek runs per │
   │ (prints none) │               │ element       │
   └───────────────┘               └───────────────┘


SKIP OPTIMIZATION (JAVA 9+): SIZED STREAM + count()

   List.of(a,b,c).stream().peek(print).count()
            │
            ▼
   ┌────────────────────┐
   │ size known = 3     │  ──▶  returns 3
   │ elements NOT walked│       peek NEVER invoked
   └────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When you need to watch a stream without disturbing it, peek is the right tool. It applies a side effect, usually logging, to each element as it flows past, then passes that same element downstream unchanged. It is intermediate and lazy, so the consumer runs only as a terminal operation pulls elements through, and only for the elements that actually reach the peek stage. A peek placed after a filter therefore sees just the survivors, which is exactly what makes it useful for auditing.

In our work at the National Bank of India, Priya from compliance wanted an audit trail of which high earners passed a salary filter, without changing the report's output. Rajesh dropped a peek right after the filter to log each passing employee, and the mapping and collection downstream produced the identical list of names as before. The camera watched the belt; it never touched a form.

The reason peek must stay advisory is that an optimizing pipeline can legally skip it. Since Java 9, a sized stream ending in count returns the size without traversing elements, so any upstream peek never fires. That is a documented optimization, not a bug, which is precisely why it is dangerous: the code looks correct and often works until a terminal operation or a JDK upgrade changes how the stream is traversed.

So the discipline is clear. Use peek for debugging and lightweight, non-essential auditing that you could delete with no loss of correctness. Put real transformations in map, and put guaranteed terminal side effects in forEach or a collector. In a parallel stream, make the peek consumer thread-safe, because it runs on many threads and the log order is not fixed.

Remember one sentence: peek is a window you look through, not a desk you work at, so never trust it with anything the program must not lose.
